abstract: Aging is associated with gastrointestinal dysfunction, yet the cellular and molecular changes underlying aging of the enteric nervous system (ENS), the cellular network that controls gut motility and digestion, remain poorly characterized. Here, we investigated whether enteric neurons show canonical hallmarks of aging in mice and humans. We assessed age-related changes in enteric neurons of the jejunum and colon in mice aged 2, 13-15, and 22-24 months using immunofluorescence, transmission electron microscopy, calcium imaging, and network morphology analysis, and compared selected markers between young and aged human gut tissue. Enteric neurons accumulated DNA damage with age in both the jejunum and colon, with nitrergic neurons exhibiting a greater burden of damage than cholinergic neurons. Increased H3K9me3-DAPI colocalization, consistent with senescence-associated heterochromatin foci, was already seen at 15 months in both regions, revealing a potentially early driver of age-related gut changes. At 24 months, colonic neuron numbers decreased, while average neuronal soma size was increased and approximately 25-30% of neurons expressed cytoplasmic p21, a marker of senescence. Aged neurons showed enlarged, less circular mitochondria and increased pPDH immunoreactivity, indicative of declining neuronal activity. Consistent with remodeling of myenteric plexus architecture, neuronal calcium responses increased upon electrical stimulation while decreasing after agonist application. DSS-induced colitis did not reproduce the DNA damage, heterochromatin, or p21 changes seen with age, implying a direct role in the latter. Human aged enteric neurons showed higher {gamma}H2AX and H3K9me3 intensities. These data demonstrate that enteric neurons develop a senescence-like phenotype with age, and identify neuronal senescence as an underexplored aspect of ENS aging.
